q: What is the primary purpose of the scope document and rules of engagement in a penetration test?
opts: Administrative paperwork required by the client
Your legal protection as a tester
A technical checklist of tools to use
A marketing document for the client
exp: As covered in Session 4: the scope document and rules of engagement are your legal protection - not bureaucracy. They define what you are authorised to test, keeping you on the right side of the Computer Misuse Act.

q: What is the main benefit of following a repeatable penetration testing lifecycle?
opts: It makes the report look professional
It allows you to charge more for each engagement
It keeps the methodology consistent and defensible across any organisation
It reduces the number of tools you need to use
exp: Session 4 explained that the lifecycle is repeatable, meaning you can conduct a pen test in the same professional manner for any organisation. This keeps you professional and legally protected.

q: Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, what is the maximum penalty for the Section 1 offence of unauthorised access to computer material?
opts: 1 year imprisonment
2 years imprisonment
5 years imprisonment
10 years imprisonment
exp: Session 5 covered the CMA 1990 sections in detail. Section 1 (unauthorised access) carries a maximum penalty of 2 years. Section 2 (with intent to commit further offences) is 5 years, and Section 3 (impairing a computer) is 10 years.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences?
opts: Section 1
Section 2
Section 3
Section 3ZA
exp: As taught in Session 5: Section 2 concerns unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences, with a maximum penalty of 5 years. Section 3 covers acts intended to impair a computer (10 years), and Section 3ZA (introduced by the Serious Crime Act 2015) covers acts causing serious damage.

q: Which UK Act was introduced in 2015 and added Section 3ZA to the Computer Misuse Act, covering acts causing serious damage?
opts: Police and Justice Act 2006
Investigatory Powers Act 2016
Serious Crime Act 2015
Data Protection Act 2018
exp: Session 5 specifically noted that Section 3ZA was introduced by the Serious Crime Act 2015. It covers unauthorised acts that cause or create a significant risk of serious damage.

q: What does CVSS stand for, and what is it used for in penetration testing?
opts: Common Vulnerability Severity Score - rates the difficulty of exploitation
Common Vulnerability Scoring System - a universally recognised way to score vulnerability severity
Cyber Vulnerability Security Standard - a UK government framework
Critical Vulnerability Scanning System - an automated scanning tool
exp: Session 5 demonstrated the CVSS calculator live. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is the universally recognised method for scoring vulnerability severity. Jon emphasised that if a client asks how you scored a vulnerability, you must be able to say you used CVSS - it means the same thing in Kathmandu as it does in the UK.

q: Why is CVSS important to use when reporting vulnerability severity to a client?
opts: It is required by GDPR for all security assessments
It automatically patches vulnerabilities once scored
It is universally recognised, so the score means the same thing to any client anywhere in the world
It is the only scoring system accepted by CREST
exp: As Jon explained in Session 5: CVSS is universally recognised - a score you produce in the UK means the same thing to a client in Kathmandu. This shared language is exactly why pen testers must be able to explain and use it.

q: What ICMP type does the ping command send as an echo request?
opts: ICMP Type 0
ICMP Type 3
ICMP Type 8
ICMP Type 11
exp: Session 3 explained that ping uses ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) Type 8, which is an echo request. Jon noted this is exactly the kind of detail CREST will test in the multiple choice exam.

q: In Nmap, what does the -sn flag do?
opts: Performs a stealth SYN scan on all ports
Performs a ping scan (host discovery only, no port scanning)
Scans for service versions on open ports
Runs all default NSE scripts against a target
exp: Covered in Session 1 (Lab B4A): -sn is Nmap's ping scan / host discovery flag. It sends probes to find which hosts are up without scanning ports. This is the first step in network sweeping.

q: In Nmap, what does the -PE flag tell Nmap to use as its host discovery probe?
opts: TCP SYN probe on port 443
UDP probe on port 53
ICMP echo request (ping)
ARP broadcast
exp: Session 1 introduced Nmap flags during Lab B4A. -PE tells Nmap to send ICMP echo requests (pings) for host discovery, equivalent to a traditional ping sweep.

q: In Nmap, what does the -sS flag perform?
opts: A full TCP connect scan
A TCP SYN (stealth) scan
A service version detection scan
An SNMP scan
exp: Covered across sessions: -sS is Nmap's TCP SYN scan, also called a stealth scan. It sends a SYN packet and listens for a SYN/ACK response without completing the three-way handshake, making it less likely to appear in application logs.

q: In Nmap, what does the -sC flag do?
opts: Performs a stealth connect scan
Runs the default set of Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts
Scans only common ports
Counts the number of open ports found
exp: Session 4 introduced NSE scripting. -sC runs Nmap's default NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine) scripts against discovered services. These scripts can enumerate additional information like HTTP titles, SSL certificates, and service details.

q: What is ARP, and why is it useful in network reconnaissance?
opts: Address Resolution Protocol - maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network
Automated Recon Protocol - a hacking tool for scanning hosts
Advanced Routing Protocol - used to find network routes
Application Response Protocol - measures server response times
exp: Session 2 covered ARP caches as part of passive recon. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses within a local network segment. Viewing the ARP cache can reveal which hosts a machine has recently communicated with.

q: What is Wireshark used for in network reconnaissance?
opts: Scanning open ports on remote hosts
Capturing and analysing network traffic packets
Exploiting vulnerabilities in web applications
Generating reports from Nmap output
exp: Session 2 introduced Wireshark as a passive recon tool. Wireshark is a packet capture and analysis tool - it allows a tester to passively observe network traffic without actively probing hosts.

q: What is the key difference between passive and active reconnaissance?
opts: Passive recon uses commercial tools; active recon uses free tools
Passive recon gathers information without directly interacting with the target; active recon involves direct interaction
Passive recon is illegal without authorisation; active recon is always legal
Passive recon only works on internal networks; active recon works on the internet
exp: Covered in Sessions 2 and 6: passive reconnaissance gathers information without directly contacting or interacting with the target. Active reconnaissance involves sending probes or traffic to the target. CREST exam questions often test this distinction - reviewing public DNS records without contacting the target is passive recon.

q: What is banner grabbing?
opts: Capturing screenshots of a target web application
Intercepting authentication tokens during login
Connecting to a service on an open port to read the information it advertises about itself
Downloading the HTTP headers from a web server
exp: Session 1 demonstrated banner grabbing live during the lab. Banner grabbing involves connecting to a service running on an open port and reading the information (banner) the service advertises - such as the software name and version. Jon called it an 'advertisement banner' the service broadcasts when you connect.

q: What service runs on TCP port 21?
opts: SSH (Secure Shell)
FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)
SMB (Server Message Block)
exp: Port numbers were covered repeatedly across sessions. TCP port 21 is used by FTP (File Transfer Protocol). Jon noted it is a primitive but still widely deployed protocol - banner grabbing FTP services reveals version information.

q: What service typically runs on TCP port 22?
opts: FTP
Telnet
SSH (Secure Shell)
SMTP
exp: Covered across multiple sessions. TCP port 22 is used by SSH (Secure Shell). Jon explained that SSH provides an interactive shell on a remote system and is commonly found on Linux servers.

q: What service runs on TCP port 80?
opts: HTTPS
FTP
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)
SNMP
exp: Covered across sessions. TCP port 80 is used by HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), the unencrypted web protocol. HTTPS runs on port 443.

q: What service runs on TCP port 443?
opts: HTTP
FTP over TLS
HTTPS (HTTP over TLS/SSL)
SNMP
exp: Covered across sessions. TCP port 443 is used by HTTPS (HTTP Secure) - HTTP traffic encrypted with TLS/SSL. When enumerating web services, finding port 443 open indicates a web server with encryption.

q: What service runs on TCP port 445, and what is it used for?
opts: RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol for graphical remote access
DNS - Domain Name Service for name resolution
SMB - Server Message Block, used to share files and printers across Microsoft networks
NFS - Network File Share used in Unix environments
exp: Session 3 (and Session 6's quiz) covered this directly. TCP port 445 is SMB (Server Message Block), which Microsoft uses to share files, folders, and printers across networks. Jon noted this is the protocol WannaCry exploited.

q: What is SMB, and what notorious malware exploited a vulnerability in it?
opts: Simple Mail Block - exploited by Mirai
Server Message Block - exploited by WannaCry
Secure Message Broker - exploited by NotPetya
System Management Bus - exploited by Stuxnet
exp: Session 3 explained: SMB (Server Message Block) is the protocol Microsoft uses to share resources across a network. WannaCry exploited a vulnerability in SMB (EternalBlue) to spread across networks in 2017, causing massive global disruption.

q: What service runs on UDP port 161?
opts: DNS
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)
NTP (Network Time Protocol)
DHCP
exp: Session 4 and Session 6 both covered this, with Session 6 using it as a quiz question. SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) runs on UDP port 161. Jon specifically noted it uses UDP, not TCP, and that CREST exam questions test this.

q: In SNMPv1, what are 'community strings'?
opts: Encrypted passwords used to authenticate network administrators
The equivalent of passwords used to authenticate access to SNMP - typically 'public' for read and 'private' for write
Network addresses used to group SNMP devices
Commands used to query SNMP-enabled devices
exp: Session 6 taught this in detail: Community strings are SNMPv1's simple authentication mechanism - they function like passwords. The default community string for read-only access is public; for write access it is private. These defaults are rarely changed, making SNMP a frequent finding in pen tests.

q: What is the default SNMPv1 community string for read-only access to a device?
opts: admin
private
public
community
exp: Session 6 explained SNMPv1 community strings directly. The default read-only community string is public. The default write community string is private. These originate from the days when networks were used only by academics and security was not a concern.

q: What is an SMB null session?
opts: A failed SMB connection caused by a misconfigured firewall
An SMB connection established without providing a username or password, historically allowed by Microsoft for network administration
An encrypted SMB session with no data transmitted
An SMB connection over an unencrypted Wi-Fi network
exp: Session 5 explained SMB null sessions: Microsoft originally allowed null sessions - connections to SMB without a username or password - so that lazy network administrators could access resources without credentials. On older or misconfigured systems, this allows an attacker to enumerate password policies, shares, and user accounts without authenticating.

q: What does DNS stand for, and what does it do?
opts: Dynamic Network Service - assigns IP addresses automatically
Domain Name System - translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses
Distributed Network Scanning - a technique for mapping large networks
Data Network Standard - a protocol for transferring files
exp: DNS was covered extensively across the sessions. DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses. Port 53 is used for DNS queries. Understanding DNS is essential for both recon and understanding how the internet works.

q: What does a /24 subnet mask mean in terms of available hosts?
opts: 24 usable host addresses
254 usable host addresses (256 minus network and broadcast)
1024 usable host addresses
It depends on the IP class
exp: Subnetting was covered across sessions including during the Nmap labs. A /24 subnet provides 256 addresses total (2^8), with 254 usable host addresses (the network address .0 and broadcast address .255 are reserved). When running a host discovery scan, a /24 means scanning up to 254 potential hosts.

q: What does the Linux command 'ip a' show you?
opts: Active network connections to remote hosts
All running processes on the system
The network interface configuration including IP addresses
Authentication logs for the system
exp: Linux CLI commands were practised in the Kali CLI Networking Orientation Lab (Sessions 1 and 2). 'ip a' (ip address) shows the network interface configuration, including IP addresses assigned to each interface - essential for understanding your position on a network during a test.

q: What is Shodan, and how does a penetration tester use it?
opts: A port scanner similar to Nmap but designed for internal networks
A search engine that indexes internet-connected devices and their open ports and banners
A web application vulnerability scanner
A tool for capturing wireless network traffic
exp: Session 4 introduced Shodan with a live demonstration (Shodan bingo). Shodan is a search engine that indexes internet-connected devices, showing their open ports, service banners, and other information. It allows passive reconnaissance of targets without directly scanning them.

q: Why can't you use Nmap to scan the IP address 192.168.0.2 from across the internet?
opts: Because Nmap doesn't support scanning IP addresses starting with 192
Because 192.168.0.2 is a private IP address and is not routable over the public internet
Because port scanning is illegal without a firewall exception
Because Nmap requires a VPN connection to scan any target
exp: Session 4 used this exact scenario as a teaching point. 192.168.x.x is a private IP address range (RFC 1918) and is not routable over the public internet. Jon explained that CREST exam questions will try to catch you out with this - you cannot reach a private IP from the internet because routers will not forward those packets.

q: What is a significant security risk of developers using public GitHub repositories for their code?
opts: GitHub automatically publishes all commits to social media
GitHub limits file sizes, forcing developers to split sensitive data
Developers accidentally commit credentials, passwords, and API keys alongside their code, making them publicly accessible
GitHub does not support two-factor authentication
exp: Session 6 covered GitHub recon in depth with a live demonstration. Developers frequently accidentally commit credentials, passwords, and API keys to public repositories. Jon showed that searching GitHub for the word 'password' returns millions of results - a goldmine for a penetration tester doing passive recon.

q: In the context of GitHub recon, what does 'forking a repository' mean?
opts: Downloading all commits from a repository's history
Creating your own copy of someone else's repository to work on independently
Merging two repositories into one
Deleting a repository from GitHub
exp: Session 6 explained GitHub concepts while covering credential exposure. Forking a repository creates your own independent copy of it, allowing you to clone it locally and work on it. Jon mentioned the deliberate insecure lab repo and suggested students fork it for practice.

q: A tester reviews public DNS records without contacting the target organisation. What type of reconnaissance is this?
opts: Active reconnaissance
Credential testing
Network scanning
Passive reconnaissance
exp: Session 6 used this exact question in the live quiz. Reviewing public DNS records without contacting the target is passive reconnaissance - you are gathering information from publicly available sources without directly interacting with the target's systems.

q: In the context of penetration testing, what should you always ask yourself about every technique and piece of information?
opts: How much would this cost to exploit commercially?
What would an attacker do with this information?
How quickly can this be automated?
Which CVSS score does this technique belong to?
exp: Session 3 emphasised the attacker mindset throughout. Jon stated explicitly: 'Everything we talk about tonight, everything we do in a lab, I want you to think about what would an attacker do with this information?' This is the core mindset of a penetration tester - understanding how knowledge can be misused.

q: Using the driving analogy Jon used in Session 3, what does Module A (methodology/law) represent, and what does Module B (technical skills) represent?
opts: Module A is the engine; Module B is the highway code
Module A is the highway code (rules); Module B is sitting behind the wheel (how the engine works)
Module A is the MOT certificate; Module B is learning to drive
Module A is the road map; Module B is the destination
exp: Session 3 introduced this analogy: Module A is the highway code - the rules and law. Module B is sitting behind the wheel and understanding how the engine actually works. Jon explained that hacking is fundamentally about understanding the mechanics of how things work, not just following rules.

q: What are IoT devices and why are they particularly vulnerable from a security perspective?
opts: Internet of Things devices - they are vulnerable because they use strong encryption that is hard to audit
Internet of Things devices - they are frequently connected to public networks, rarely updated or patched, and may have no traditional user interface
Internal of Things devices - they are vulnerable because they use proprietary protocols
Internet of Tools devices - they are vulnerable because they expose APIs to the internet
exp: Session 4 opened with an IoT/SCADA news discussion. IoT (Internet of Things) devices are vulnerable because they are often publicly accessible, rarely updated or patched, and sometimes have no traditional graphical interface. Jon used internet-connected fridges as an example - an attack surface most people haven't considered.

q: What is SCADA and where would you typically find it?
opts: Secure Cloud Architecture for Data Assets - found in banking systems
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition - specialist industrial control systems found in power stations, water plants, railways, and factories
Security Compliance and Audit framework - found in government organisations
Scalable Computing and Data Analysis - found in data centres
exp: Session 4 discussed SCADA as part of the IoT/OT news segment. SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) refers to industrial control systems found in critical infrastructure like power stations, hydroelectric plants, water treatment, and railways. Jon noted that OT/SCADA security is a growing specialism with high demand.
